newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria draws up battle lines over NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Austria draws up battle lines over NATO entry.

text.p: Austria's two governing parties drew up battles lines over NATO on Wednesday with conservatives in favour of membership of the Western military alliance and Social Democrats opposed to ditching neutrality.
While the ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party locked horns, opposition parties joined the fray and lined up behind both camps.

The far-right Freedom Party, a staunch supporter of NATO entry, urged the People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel to remain firm, saying that together they had a majority in parliament to vote for NATO membership.
"(The People's Party) should finally have the courage to make a clear decision over Austria's joining NATO," Freedom Party defence spokesman Herbert Scheibner said in a statement.

The conservatives and the far right have voted together in parliament before, but an alliance over such a sensitive issue as NATO would bring down the government and did not appear immediately likely.

But conservative Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend on Wednesday reinforced a message he made in Paris on Tuesday, saying it was now only a matter of time before Austria applied for membership of the 16-nation alliance.
Austrian news agency APA quoted Fasslabend as saying no-one in government was any longer against NATO entry in principle.
"The new European security structures are being formed...If everyone agrees in principle where the train is headed, no-one should miss it," he said on a visit to the town of Graz.
Social Democrat parliamentary speaker Heinz Fischer swiftly rejected Fasslabend's remarks, insisting there was no government agreement "in principle" on joining NATO.

"The coalition agreement is open to several options, including maintaining neutrality and not joining NATO, which I personally believe to be the most sensible and probable option," Fischer said in a statement.
Leftist Greens said Austria's neutrality law had to stay.
Chancellor Viktor Klima and his dominant Social Democrats insist the time is not ripe for full NATO membership.
Fasslabend disagrees. "Waiting cannot be the theme running through Austria's security and foreign policy. We should have been in NATO before our neighbours," he told the Kurier daily.

Schuessel caused a stir last month when he backed NATO entry during a visit to Brussels. Mindful of the fragility of the coalition, he backtracked on returning home, saying he was speaking as a conservative politician not as foreign minister.

The NATO debate surfaced in Austria after the country joined the EU in 1994 and has intensified as the alliance moves closer to admitting former Warsaw Pact states as new members at a summit in Madrid in July.
Hungary and the Czech Republic -- two of Austria's neighbours -- and Poland are the frontrunners for the first wave of NATO expansion. Slovenia, another of Austria's neighbours, may also be included.

John Roper, associate fellow at the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London, said it apppeared increasingly likely that the next round of NATO expansion may not be aimed at former communist states, but at "the EU neutrals", Austria, Finland and Sweden.
"We could see Austria, Sweden and Finland in a new enlargement, possibly next year or in 1999," Roper said. "We would then have a closer symmetry of NATO and the EU."
